EXCLUSIVE: Indonesian filmmaker Edwin has revealed the five young leads for his upcoming feature, Dancing With My Shadow ( Menari Dengan Bayangan : Evakuasi ), inspired by the album of the same name from Hindia .

Produced by Palari Films , the coming-of-age drama marks a return to youth-focused stories for Edwin following horror film Sleep No More (2026), which premiered in Berlinale Special Midnight earlier this year, and darkly comic action romance Vengeance Is Mine, All Other Pay Cash , which won the Golden Leopard at Locarno film festival in 2021.

Based on the album by singer-songwriter Baskara Putra (a.k.a. Hindia), Dancing With My Shadow will star a mix of rising talent and familiar faces, including Rafly Altama, known for Riri Riza's Rangga Cinta , and Hyori Mika, who stars in Palari Films’ recent Tokyo prize winner Jani Be Good . blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); } Related Stories Documentary Kate Middleton Documentary 'Heal' Set At BBC & NBC; Special About Princess' Three Peaks Challenge & Cancer Journey Gets Release Date & Trailer News Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days

Also joining the cast is Muzakki Ramdhan, a former child actor from well-known genre films such as Gundala and Satan's Slave 2: Communion , who already has more than 30 films under his belt.

Newer faces in the young cast include Daffa Saputra, an actor and fashion model for whom this is his first significant film role, and Freya, a member of the JKT48 idol girl group, who started her acting career in horror hit Dominion Of Darkness and family drama A Brother And 7 Siblings .

The cast is being revealed tonight at the final of the DBL Jakarta Series, Indonesia’s biggest high school basketball league, the world where the story takes place.

Released in 2019, Hindia’s Menari Dengan Bayangan became the soundtrack of a generation, touching on subjects that young Indonesians rarely talk about openly: anxieties around growing up, pressure from home, and the fear of being left behind. It holds the record as the most-streamed Indonesian-language album on Spotify, and still regularly appears on the platform’s weekly Top Albums chart in Indonesia.

The team behind the film explain that the album’s themes have been reworked into an original story, “with the music serving as an emotional map rather than a script”. Written by Winnie Benjamin, the story follows a quiet teenager, still grieving his father, who becomes the photographer for his high school’s rowdy basketball supporters club. Behind chants and chaos, he finds friendship, first love and a group of kids quietly learning how to survive. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Produced by Palari Films’ Muhammad Zaidy and Meiske Taurisia, the film will be executive produced by Baskara Putra, Mira Lesmana and Dian Sastrowardoyo, with music by Petra Sihombing and Enrico Octaviano.

Baskara will also appear in the film as himself performing on a concert stage. Commenting on the project he said: “This album feels like my own child. I’ve always wanted my albums to take on new forms, but handing it to someone else was scary. Then I realized the film shouldn’t be my life story. It should be a new story born from the same feelings. Edwin has always filmed young people honestly, without looking down on them. That’s what these songs needed."

For Edwin, the project marks a return to youth stories a decade after 2017 coming-of-age drama Posesif , which won a Citra Award for Best Director. “Agra spends most of the film behind a camera, deciding what to frame and what to leave out. I think that’s how many of us lived our teenage years,” Edwin said. “The stands are full of noise and bodies, but everyone there is carrying something they don’t talk about. I wanted to stay close enough to feel it.”

Zaidy said: “From Posesif to Ali & Ratu Ratu Queens and Dear David , and now Menari Dengan Bayangan: Evakuasi , we keep coming back to coming-of-age stories. There’s always a fascinating crossroads in them. They feel familiar to so many people, yet there’s always a sense of liberation and empathy for people going through a transition in their lives. That stays relevant, even for adult audiences.

Dancing With My Shadow is being lined up for an Indonesian theatrical release in summer 2027.

articles.title: 'Fatherland' Review: Thomas Mann and His Daughter Travel Across Germany in 1949 in Pawel Pawlikowski's Meticulous Time Machine of a Drama
articles.summary: The matter-of-fact seduction of Pawlikowski’s filmmaking lies in how he stages everything with a coolly objective authenticity. In "Fatherland," he lends this historical moment a time-machine quality, so that we feel we’re right there, in Germany in 1949, seeing the sands of history shift. Pawlikowski is ruminating on moral choice, and he’s also ruminating on God.
articles.content:
In the elegant, silvery, and fascinating " Fatherland ," the Polish director Pawel Pawlikowski presents the latest chapter in what feels, after "Ida" and "Cold War," like a trilogy (though maybe it will be a quartet; his last feature was released eight years ago, and he’s the furthest thing possible from a predictable filmmaker).

The movies in this unofficial series are quite different from one another, though they’re linked in striking ways. Each one is set in Europe during the Cold War; each takes on political and historical themes of unabashed momentousness; each is told in meticulously framed, lustrous black-and-white images that Pawlikowski, who started out as a documentary filmmaker, cuts together with the stark precision of a cinematic coffee-table photography book; and each, in its monochromatically austere way, falls into the category of art-object-as-awards-bait ("Ida" won the 2013 Academy Award for best foreign language film; "Cold War" was nominated for three Oscars in 2018, including best director). blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Taylor Swift, Jaafar Jackson, ‘The Odyssey’ Among Hollywood Music in Media Awards Winners Anne Hathaway to Receive American Riviera Award at Santa Barbara International Film Festival

"Fatherland," set in 1949, is about a journey taken by Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika, an actress and writer, from West Germany to East Germany — the twin ideological poles of the Cold War. The movie feels linked to the grand themes of "Ida" and "Cold War," notably the Holocaust and the rise of European Communism. Yet what unites these films most, and is the defining aesthetic of "Fatherland," is how Pawlikowski observes the drama with a blend of intimacy and lordly detachment. "Fatherland" is an incisive and ambitious movie that wants to lay bare the torn soul of Germany after World War II. It’s also a portrait of family demons and literary celebrity. The film, as photographed by Łukasz Żal, has been made in a spirit of nearly fetishistic meticulousness; it’s as subtle as a fine wine. Yet "Fatherland," as an experience, is so steeped in ideas that in the end it’s more heady than haunting. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

It opens on a note of discordant bitterness: Klaus Mann (August Diehl), Mann’s dissolute author son, is speaking on the phone with his sister, Erika ( Sandra Hüller ), declaring the state of cynical despair he has arrived at. We’ll never totally learn how he got that way, but his morose funk acts as an offbeat warning about the world that’s coming.

His father, Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler), the legendary author of "Death in Venice" and "The Magic Mountain," is on hand to issue warnings as well, but of a grander variety. He’s a literary rock star to his fellow Germans (who line up to see him wherever he goes), and we watch him give several speeches — the first in Frankfurt, the robust city that’s under the sway of the Americans (one of the first people Mann meets there is a representative of the relatively new Central Intelligence Agency), and then one in Weimar, which is under Communist control, though it’s the place where the great Johann Wolfgang von Goethe spent his adult life, and in Mann’s eyes Goethe is a god; that’s why he wants to go there. The thrust of Mann’s speeches is that Germany, after its plunge into evil, must engage in a spiritual reckoning, a new embrace of humanity, the kind that coursed through Goethe’s writing. He says Goethe "resisted the German romantic death cult" and in so doing provided the answer to "the German problem." That, in a way, is what "Fatherland" is about: the question of how a lost society can heal itself.

Mann is presented as the Last Civilized Man of a vanishing era, whose words, spoken before audiences of officials, are lofty and inspiring. But will they make a difference? Mann, as we learn, is a U.S. citizen who lives in California (and is told that he may not be allowed to return there if he visits Weimar and shows any solidarity with the Communist government). But the movie also suggests that he has demons closer to home. Hanns Zischler, in a thick mustache, looks a lot like Mann, though it may not be a coincidence that he also bears a resemblance to Victor Sjöström, the star of Ingmar Bergman’s "Wild Strawberries." "Fatherland" comes close to fashioning itself as a companion piece to that film, with Mann as the stately but "cold" figure of learned authority, whose daughter tries to cut through his diffident façade. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The two actors are pitch-perfect, with Hüller’s Erika tart yet polite, reigning herself in until she can’t take the old man’s buried narcissism anymore, at which point she lets her feelings fly. That’s a terrific scene, but "Fatherland" could have used a few more like it. The section of the movie set in Weimer provokes a chill, because we see that the Communist officials believe in their vision of a "utopia," even as the film cues us to see that they’re not only deluded but deceptive. (At one point, Mann learns that the nearby site of the former Buchenwald concentration camp now houses political prisoners.) The movie is letting us know what totalitarianism looks like when it’s on the rise. That Mann and his daughter, at a posh Frankfurt hotel party, glimpse so many remnants of the Nazi era — including Erika’s ex-husband, who collaborated with the regime — is another portent of darkness.

The matter-of-fact seduction of Pawlikowski’s filmmaking lies in how he stages everything with a coolly objective authenticity. In "Fatherland," he lends this historical moment a time-machine quality, so that we feel we’re right there, in the ruins of Germany in 1949, seeing the sands of history shift. Pawlikowski is ruminating on moral choice, and he’s also ruminating on God. The final scene, in which Mann and Erika visit the church where Johann Sebastian Bach had his first appointment (they hear "Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring" played on the church’s ancient pipe organ), speaks to both. Yet Pawlikowski, whose best film, in my book, remains the rapturous hot-house romance "My Summer of Love" (2004), works in such a deliberate way that as compelling as "Fatherland" is, it’s a movie that has already thought out everything it wants us to feel.

articles.title: I Think Mephisto Is Going to Be the Next MCU Big Bad and the Comics Are Proving It
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Comics The lifecycle of the Marvel Cinematic Universe has been very interesting. There was once a time where if you typed a negative word and the letters "MCU" in the same sentence, you would get dogpiled by an army of teens and twentysomethings, none of whom had ever read comics or experienced anything Marvel pre-2008 but […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The lifecycle of the Marvel Cinematic Universe has been very interesting. There was once a time where if you typed a negative word and the letters "MCU" in the same sentence, you would get dogpiled by an army of teens and twentysomethings, none of whom had ever read comics or experienced anything Marvel pre-2008 but all of whom wanted you to know that they were bigger Marvel fans than you. The entire nerd side of the Internet was run by MCU fans in the United States for years, with only manga and anime being as beloved. It was during this time when wiki-readers (because for some reason, MCU fans just refuse to read actual comics) started to dig into the bones of the Marvel Universe to figure out where they were going things next. This led many of them to find Mephisto and suddenly, they were predicting that he was the big bad of everything.

WandaVision was supposedly going to end with a battle between her and Mephisto. Then it was thought that he might be behind her going crazy. MCU fans were doing their best to manifest this idea of Mephisto in the MCU, which is all the more amusing that his debut was such a nothing burger for both the franchise and fandom. With Avengers: Doomsday on the way, the Multiverse Saga is about to come to its culmination, and I have a rather bold prediction of what's coming next: Mephisto is going to be the big bad of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Why you might ask? Because I'm sure he's about to become the main villain of a major Marvel Comics event.

So, this is going to seem like circular logic, but by the time I finish this, I'll have made my argument. So, let's start at the beginning. Captain America (Vol. 14) has been one of the most important Marvel titles of 2025 and 2026. It's helped build the newest volume of Avengers , acting as the kick-off for Avengers: Armageddon with "Doom's Shadow". The next story, "Hell's Angel", took Cap to Mephisto's realm, where he found Doom, dead since the end of One World Under Doom . The two of them battled Red Skull and Mephisto, leading Doom to defeat the infernal demon lord and take his place.

Mephisto is a monstrous entity , but one thing he's not is the devil. Doom doesn't run Hell now, he just runs a subsidiary of it. Mephisto is all about making deals and stealing souls and the first thing Doom did was invalidate all of those deals, including the one that ended Peter Parker's marriage. Doom didn't kill Mephisto; he's still around, something that fans learned in Avengers #1, which spun out Avengers: Armageddon and Captain America (Vol. 14).

This issue was about two things – a new group of Avengers coming together from the ashes of the old (if they hadn't have tried a New Avengers reboot last year because of Thunderbolts* , that's the title they should have went with for the book) as New York City starts to go crazy, all because of Mephisto's deals expiring. The devil makes a shadowy appearance in the book and it feels like one of the main plots of the comic is going to be this new team of Avengers dealing with Mephisto.

It's pretty easy to predict things at Marvel Comics. Marvel has put it self into a cycle of events and I can teach you how to identify them. Basically, if an A-list writer gets put on a big A-list series, they are building towards an event. Phillip Kennedy Johnson came to Hulk, we get a Hulk event a few years later. Jed MacKay has written two X-Men events and one Avengers event when he worked on both books. Zdarsky wrote one for Daredevil and just got done with Avengers: Armageddon . I'm pretty sure we're going to get a third out of him, this one a Mephisto one.

So, I know what you're thinking at this point – "David, you haven't explained how all of this effects the MCU." To which I say we've gotten there. So, if you're a fan of Marvel Comics, there are two words you hate: MCU synergy. Basically, Marvel thinks that since the MCU has more fans, if they make the comics more like the movies, they'll read comics. This never happens; the only thing it does is anger comic fans. However, that synergy does go both ways, because Kevin Feige doesn't like to hire anyone with an original idea for superheroes.

If you look at the history of the MCU, you can point at everything they've copied from the comics. MCU writers don't really come up with their own stories, they just smush together a couple of different stories, add in some cliche sarcastic quips, ruin a classic costume, sprinkle in a really lame ending action scene, and then call it a movie. Now, yes, that's overly harsh, but there has been no original story in the MCU. Not once. All of them take ideas from the comics, and often do them in more cliche ways to appeal to the largest possible audience, and that's just the way it is.

Mephisto has rarely been a big villain in the comics so I think that MCU fans had something to do with his latest push. There were a solid couple of years there where MCU fans were predicting that Mephisto was going to be in everything. Kevin Feige is all about Easter Eggs. I have problems with him as a creative, but that man loves Marvel and its fans. He now runs the whole of Marvel and I can see him orchestrating something like this as a meta Easter Egg for MCU fans who kept the faith that Mephisto would show up. It might seem a little far-fetched, but let's be real, so was the chances that the MCU would get this far.

Movie synergy is a thing that has been around since comic characters started to show up in movies, with examples like the X-Men's leather uniforms or Spider-Man's organic webshooters showing up in the past. However, the success of the MCU has been on another level and this has made synergy just about inescapable. The comics are changed all the time, to the point where I dread when the MCU adapts Avengers stories or Spider-Man stories, because I know that some of that is going to show up in the comics.

Mephisto's current story arc in the comics is almost certainly going to lead to a massive event. There's really no way it won't – Marvel is all about events. With the Multiverse Saga coming to a close, the MCU is going to need a new focus. Mephisto can be that for the next Phases of the MCU. The movies always copy the comics and if I'm correct about the upcoming Mephisto event, there's a great chance that Sasha Baron Cohen is going to become a major MCU villain in the future.

Do you think Mephisto's story is leading to an event comic? Do you think the MCU will pull the trigger on making him the big bad? Sound off in the comment section below.

With the legal deadline for a termination drawing near, she picks up odd jobs to cover the cost, working her way through a bleak job market and backstreet clinics before landing on the campaign trail of a local politician. Pura says she found that many women she met had been through abortions alone, for lack of money or support from family and society. "While there is institutional support, it is quite biased. Who gets to go to a public hospital and who can pay for it at a private clinic?"

Pura is co-producing with Kharcha Paani Talkies. Pura says she wants the film to bring into the open "the conversations I have had with women in living rooms, washrooms, boardrooms and in the waiting area of gynaec clinics." Women, she says, cope with sexual violence "with grief, perseverance, impulsivity but most importantly – lots of dark humor – hence I've kept the tone of the film that way too. This film should be cathartic for women and hopefully informative for the uninitiated."

A Platform Busan alum this year, Pura has developed shows, films and documentaries for Netflix, Amazon Studios, JioHotstar, the British Asian Trust, USAID and Outlook Traveller. She is completing the Punjabi short "Kosi Sardi" (Are You Mad At Me), about two Punjabi women in their 80s, a tenant and her landlady, whose friendship breaks down.

articles.title: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Makes a Major Mistake by Removing One of the Book's Most Horrifying Details
articles.summary: In 2025, Suzanne Collins gave The Hunger Games fans something they had long wanted with Sunrise on the Reaping: the story of Haymitch Abernathy’s 50th Hunger Games, aka the Second Quarter Quell. It’s a story that not only showed Haymitch’s origin story, if you can call it that, but shined a light on just how […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google In 2025, Suzanne Collins gave The Hunger Games fans something they had long wanted with Sunrise on the Reaping: the story of Haymitch Abernathy’s 50th Hunger Games, aka the Second Quarter Quell. It’s a story that not only showed Haymitch’s origin story, if you can call it that, but shined a light on just how dark and brutal the Capitol really is with themes of political manipulation, totalitarian control, and the power of propaganda . The story also showed the initial sparks of revolution that would eventually ignite with Katniss and her games and it is one that fans were eager to see play out on screen as well. Now, with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping finally here and in theaters , Haymitch’s story is getting it’s due — but in telling his story, the film has made a major mistake.

Part of what makes Collins’ novel so powerful is that it doesn’t shy away from just how absolutely horrific the Games are and the disturbing lengths the powers that be in the Capitol will go to in terms of not only controlling and oppressing the Districts, but in manipulating the narrative as well. To an extent, the film gives us a glimpse at that and does it well. We see President Snow’s cruelty and manipulation, particularly in how Haymitch is made to suffer before, during, and after the Games. But there’s one character in the book that really drives home how bleak things really are and whose life — and death — leaves scars on Haymitch like no other and it’s a character who ends up so glossed over in the movie that that core horror is fully lost: Lou Lou.

Now, before I dig into why Lou Lou is the character whose life and death being sanitized (for lack of a better term) is the biggest mistake the Sunrise on the Reaping film made I want to make something clear: the handling of other significant deaths, such as Ampert, Wellie, and Maysilee also fall into the category of horrors that the movie really should have more directly adapted. But Ampert, Wellie, and Maysilee are all deaths that one would expect by nature of them being Tributes in the Games. Lou Lou’s arc is unique as she was never actually a Tribute. She was a girl stripped of her identity, tortured, brutalized, and used as a puppet of political control. He was the living embodiment of the Capitol and Snow’s evil and in many ways is the turning point of the story.

Following Louella McCoy’s death in the Tribute Parade (a death which, by the way, was far more horrific in the book), the Capitol replaces her with a body double, a young girl who resembles Louella and has clearly been tortured into mimicking Louella. She says little, only repeating that she is Louella McCoy from District 12. Because she’s obviously not, the actual District 12 tributes nickname her Lou Lou. In the movie, as in the book, Lou Lou meets her end early in the Games when she ended up smelling flowers that turned out to be poisoned. Her death was tragic and horrible on screen, but overall, Lou Lou’s entire movie arc was brief and her death felt like a natural extension of things, just another death in the Games.

The book is vastly different. Lou Lou in the book is in far worse shape when she’s presented to Haymitch. It’s clear that the girl has been starved horribly, but that the Capitol has artificially plumped her face up to hide this. It is also implied that she’s the daughter of traitors who was taken to punish them. The poor girl couldn’t really say anything useful (like in the movie, she just keeps repeating that she’s Louella McCoy) and it freaks out the other Tributes. As time passes during training ahead of the Games, Haymitch and the others discover that Lou Lou has two devices implanted into her body, one being a device in her ear where the Capitol tells her what to say and do while a pump device was implanted in her chest to push drugs into her so that she could be controlled. Both of these devices caused her great suffering. Even with this, little details about the real girl start to emerge suggesting that she’s actually from District 11, but no one knows who she really is. At one point, Lou Lou even manages to find some spark of resistance, growling in her interview with Caesar Flickerman that the Capitol will murder them to which the poor girl is swiftly punished and subdued with drugs through the pump in her chest.

Lou Lou’s death is also much more horrific in the book. While she does end up poisoned by smelling flowers, it’s not actually the poison that kills her. After stopping to smell bee balm because they reminded her of her real home, she starts choking and convulsing. Blood pours from her eyes, nose, and mouth, and the poor little girl is in horrific pain. Haymitch begs for the Gamemakers to end her suffering with the pump in her chest but they don’t. Instead, Haymitch has to pull the device from her chest to end her life.

While there are obviously things that the movie adaptation of Sunrise on the Reaping could not show in order to maintain a PG-13 rating, like the graphic nature of how Ampert and Wellie actually died, the horror and tragedy of Lou Lou is something that could have been kept and indeed needed to be. With Sunrise on the Reaping having such significant themes and messages about the totalitarian control, manipulation, propaganda, and cruelty of the Capitol and President Snow, Lou Lou in the books is a character that quite literally embodies all of the horrors that are inflicted on the Districts. She has her identity stolen, her body broken, and her very existence used and manipulated to mislead the Capitol audience of the Games while also sending a message that dissent will be silenced by any means necessary.

Lou Lou is also the catalyst for Haymitch’s defiance and the first sparks of what will eventually become a full-on rebellion. While Lou Lou was not his “sweetheart”, Haymitch came to pity and also care for Lou Lou. She sparks empathy in him and he begins to see her as one of his own for who she is even though he has no idea of her true identity. It’s her horrific death and the open cruelty shown to her in dying that forces Haymitch to essentially mercy kill the poor child that fully cements his will to take the Games down. Louella’s death was crushing but genuinely an accident. Lou Lou’s however, was a direct example of blatant cruelty — and the first attempt at the Capitol to take his humanity. By leaving this element of Lou Lou’s story out, the movie diminishes a bit of Haymitch’s journey — and it feels like a giant missed opportunity.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters now.

Now it’s your turn. Did you think the minimizing of Lou Lou’s story hurt the movie? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: I Watched Smoke Signals For The First Time, And Two Things Really Caught Me Off Guard
articles.summary: I expected a road trip comedy and got so much more.
articles.content:
Amid the various kinds of films I enjoy, coming-of-age movies hold a special place in my heart. There’s something special about a story that sees young people navigating growing pains, whether they be Black-led coming-of-age stories or those told from other perspectives. On that note, I had been meaning to watch the much revered Smoke Signals for some time, and I finally did that amid Native American Heritage Month. I’m pleased to say that not only is the movie great as promised, but it also surprised me in two ways.

Released in 1998, Smoke Signals is based on screenwriter Sherman Alexie’s The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven . The Chris Eyre-directed road trip dramedy primarily centers around two Indigenous teens – Victor Joseph (Adam Beach) and Thomas Builds-the-Fire (Evan Adams). The mismatched pair set off on a trip from their Idaho-based reservation to Phoenix, Arizona, to collect the ashes of Victor’s recently deceased father.

Alcoholism is also explored in great depth, as flashbacks show both of the Arnolds dealing with it, to the point where a young Victor destroys their beer in defiance. It’s a striking moment and serves as the wake-up call Victor’s mother, Arlene (Tantoo Cardinal), needs. Additionally, domestic abuse is a key theme, as Arnold is shown abusing Victor and Arlene on different occasions. Overall, through the Josephs, audiences get a nuanced look at dysfunctional intergenerational relationships .

Smoke Signals also has other grim moments. I mean, the film opens with a flashback to the night of a Fourth of July party, at which point Thomas’ parents are killed in a house fire. And the only reason baby Thomas survives is due to being saved by Arnold, who Thomas grows to idolize despite his faults. While the darker material caught me off guard, I truly appreciated Eyre and Alexie tackling such subject matter and doing so with some layered Indigenous characters .

Throughout the film, there’s also a heavy emphasis on the Native American tradition of oral storytelling. Much of that is thanks to Thomas, who tells stories – that vary in terms of how true they are – whether people want to hear them or not. Adams delivers these soliloquies perfectly, and they add a soulful element to the film. I particularly love when Thomas bonds over storytelling with Arnold’s Phoenix- based friend, Suzy Song (Irene Bedard), who is a badass Indigenous woman in a fairly understated way.

All in all, this keen focus on storytelling only enhances the movie, and Eyre and Alexie’s reverence for it is more than evident. It also opens the door for viewers like myself to gain a better understanding of an aspect of Native American culture we wouldn’t otherwise be privy to. As a viewer, I really enjoy being engulfed in different cultural perspectives via film and TV, and truly relish whenever nuanced stories centered on (and told by) Indigenous people are pushed to the forefront.

Responding to an audience question, Bertuccelli said she set out to adapt the Mankell book five years ago. She wrote the script and cast the film, which was due to shoot in Canada, before the pandemic brought everything to a halt.

"In fact there is a bad Canadian producer who stole the film from me," Bertuccelli said. She did not name the producer and declined to give the full account. She said she was forced to cancel the project, adding: "I worked for quite four years, five years for nothing because they stole from me, they stole, you know, the movie and I could not do it. So it was very hard."

Bertuccelli turned to the directors in the room. "It's a fight against you, against yourself, because you need to work, you need even when you are depressed or you have doubts, you need to continue, because the only thing that makes you a director is that you go on and you never, you know, you never stop your desire," she said.

She is now writing the new feature. It follows a French woman living in Mumbai who is slowly going blind and sets off on one last journey with her son, who is half Indian and half French. Bertuccelli plans to come to India to make it. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"It's my first time in India, but for so long I'm admiring your country, your culture," she said.

Bertuccelli is also finishing a second documentary alongside "The Violin Lesson," which follows Rachel Routier, a violin teacher in Pantin, outside Paris, and is headed for French cinemas after airing on France Télévisions in September. She hopes to screen "The Violin Lesson" in Mumbai in the coming weeks, along with either "The Tree" or "Since Otar Left."

During two terms as president of La Scam, the French authors' society for documentary makers, Bertuccelli created the Golden Eye documentary prize at Cannes, whose Indian winners include Payal Kapadia's "A Night of Knowing Nothing" and Shaunak Sen's "All That Breathes." She also founded La Cinémathèque du documentaire in Paris, which hopes to stage a retrospective of Indian documentary.

Asked by Kumar whether documentary carries a social responsibility, Bertuccelli said: "For sure there is a big responsibility because the film can change the life of somebody, you know?"

She pointed to "School of Babel," which followed a class for children newly arrived in France. The film was widely seen by school groups and shifted young viewers' attitudes toward immigrant classmates, she said, and it helped protect such classes at a time when some were being closed. "Because I said with this film to all the Education Ministry: 'So I made a film to show that France is great, but don't touch it. Now you can't destroy this,'" she said.

Kumar later asked where cinema stands in the age of AI. Bertuccelli allowed that the technology can be useful for small tasks, such as sound work.

"But I hate AI. Not just because, okay, it's dangerous for us, we will forget how to have memory, how to think by ourselves. Also because they steal, they stole the film, you know, they stole the author rights. But also more because it's an ecological, horrible, horrible thing," she said.

Documentary, she argued, is cinema's last line of defense, because "there is a contract with you that when you see a documentary, there is reality, there is truth." She added that "the 21st century will be the one of documentary."

Bertuccelli spent around 15 years as an assistant to directors including Krzysztof Kieślowski, Bertrand Tavernier and Otar Iosseliani before making her own documentaries. Her fiction debut, "Since Otar Left," shot in Georgia, won the Critics' Week grand prize at Cannes and the César for best first film. Her documentary work includes "School of Babel," "Latest News From the Cosmos" and "Jane Campion, the Cinema Woman." "The Tree," starring Charlotte Gainsbourg, played IFFI more than 15 years ago, but Bertuccelli could not attend as she was eight months pregnant at the time. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

She closed the session by pointing back to the Lumière brothers, whose operators traveled the world filming everyday life.

"Cinema was born documentary and it will die documentary," she said.

The life and legacy of legendary Egyptian artist Mohamed Mounir is set to be explored in a biopic spearheaded by The Film Committee at Media City Qatar .

The Film Committee has acquired the rights to document Mounir’s life story, with partners on the project set to include a leading regional studio and other partners, which have yet to be announced.

The project was announced at the Film Committee's Doha Industry Days, just hours after the Qatari body gave an update on previously announced biopic Caesar , about Syrian whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan, announcing Taim Hasan as it star. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News 'Al Hayba' Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed 'Caesar' Biopic News Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: "It's Going To Be Good For The World" - Industry Days Doha

Mounir’s career spans nearly five decades across music, film and television. His 1981 breakthrough album ‘Shababeek’ established him as one of Egypt ’s most distinctive artists, with his work characterized by its fusion of Nubian folk and Arabic pop with Western genres like jazz, blues, and reggae.

He is known to his fans across the Middle East and beyond as “El King” in reference to his 1998 album and play ‘El Malek Howwa El Malek’ ((The King is The King).

Also working in cinema, his some 20 credits including collaborations with late Egyptian filmmaker Youssef Chahine on films including Egyptian Story (1982) and Destiny, which played in Out of Competition in Cannes in 1997 and was then selected as Egypt’s Oscar entry.

Mounir was born into a Nubian family in a village in Southern Egypt, where he spent his early childhood. His family moved to Cairo, after the village was resettled due to the construction of the Aswan Dam in the 1960s, where his singing voice was discovered when he sang at a family gathering.

The Film Committee said the biopic will trace Mounir's journey from his humble beginnings to becoming one of the Arab world’s most celebrated and influential artists, revealing untold details, surprises, stories and anecdotes.

“ Bringing his story to the big screen is an opportunity to celebrate his artistry, the cultural heritage his work represents and its lasting social relevance, a story that connects generations of fans across the region and has the power to resonate with audiences around the world," he continued.

“This project also builds on our recent investment in extraordinary life stories from the region and reflects our ambition to develop a world-leading slate of biographical films that brings these stories to audiences globally.”

Alongside the feature film, plans include a behind-the-scenes documentary featuring interviews with Mounir and those who have lived and worked alongside him, as well as documenting the development and production of the biopic.

With development in the early stages, the hunt is now on for an actor to play Mounir.

articles.summary: Qatar's Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures have announced a strategic partnership to develop and co-produce a slate of films "championing visionary filmmakers and compelling stories from the Global South and beyond with an emphasis on culturally authentic storytelling and broad international appeal," they said in a statement. articles.content:
Qatar's Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures have announced a strategic partnership to develop and co-produce a slate of films "championing visionary filmmakers and compelling stories from the Global South and beyond with an emphasis on culturally authentic storytelling and broad international appeal," they said in a statement.

The Global South is a geopolitical and economic term that broadly includes countries in Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, most of Asia, and most of Oceania. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories ‘GTA 6’ Upsets Conservatives: Fox News Tells Fans to ‘Grow Up’ as Clavicular and More Manosphere Influencers Complain About Lucia Jo Koy on ‘Blue in the Face,’ Steven Spielberg, Biggie’s Mom and Learning What His Name Really Means at Long John Silver’s

The Qatar Film Committee is an official body that is part of the Media City Qatar hub and is tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry.

Founded in April 2024 by brothers Badie Ali and Hamza Ali, Chicago-based Watermelon Pictures has gained worldwide attention in its short time in business with releases such as Rashid Masharawi's "From Ground Zero," Annemarie Jacir's "Palestine 36" and Cherien Dabis' "All That’s Left of You," which were shortlisted for the best international feature Oscar, as well as Kaouther ben Hania's Oscar-nominated "The Voice of Hind Rajab."

The partnership between Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon was announced on the second day of the Doha Film Festival ’s Industry Days, which are running from Nov. 19-21.

The plan is for the pact to spawn a slate of projects developed by Watermelon spanning comedy, television, genre and drama. Financial terms were not disclosed.

"Combining Qatar's commitment to world-class filmmaking, growing production capabilities, and investment in the creative economy with Watermelon's access to leading talent, established distribution infrastructure, and deep understanding of what resonates with audiences, the collaboration aims to produce commercially compelling films with high production values and international appeal," the statement said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The plan envisions that these projects will shoot mainly in Qatar or be structured as Qatari co-productions. They will tap into the country’s growing production ecosystem and the Qatar Screen Production Incentive rebate offering up to 50% in cash, "creating opportunities for local crews, businesses and creative talent while strengthening Qatar's position as an international production hub," it noted.

“Through this partnership, we want to give filmmakers the resources to tell stories rooted in their communities and bring them to audiences around the world," Hassan Al Thawadi, the Qatari lawyer who chairs the Qatar Film Committee, said in the statement.

For Watermelon Pictures, the partnership marks a significant leap into larger-scale, mainstream production, backed by its distribution expertise.

articles.title: 5 Brilliant Movie Concepts That Deserved Better Execution (& #1 Could Have Been a Sci-Fi Classic)
articles.summary: Imagine watching a movie after reading its premise and getting your hopes up, only to reach the end and see that you either wasted your time or just watched something that could have been a thousand times better. Some films have been released with such fantastic concepts that it's extremely frustrating to find out how […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Imagine watching a movie after reading its premise and getting your hopes up, only to reach the end and see that you either wasted your time or just watched something that could have been a thousand times better. Some films have been released with such fantastic concepts that it's extremely frustrating to find out how badly they were handled . And honestly, quite a few productions of the last few years have faced backlash for exactly failing to properly develop their stories.

Maybe some of these still have their good points, and you might even consider your experience watching them to be just okay. But you can see how much more satisfying they could have been with a better-written script, right? We've picked 5 movies that are perfect examples of this. Have you seen any of them?

Old came from the brilliant mind of M. Night Shyamalan , but it's not a movie people remember so much, mainly because its execution falls so short of its potential (although, sure, some people did enjoy it). Based on the graphic novel Sandcastle , the story follows a group of tourists who discover that time moves differently on a beach: children grow up super fast, adults age right before their eyes, and even health problems progress at an alarming rate. Just imagine realizing that you could lose your entire life before you even have a chance to find a way out. The premise has huge thriller potential and could lead to some really good family conflicts, especially when it comes to how parents and children would deal with the possibility of growing old together in just a few hours.

Unfortunately, the movie doesn't make the most of these possibilities. There are a few crazy, uncomfortable moments, such as Kara's (Eliza Scanlen) accelerated pregnancy and Chrystal's (Abbey Lee) bones repeatedly breaking and rebuilding themselves, but the characters are never developed enough, and the explanation behind what's happening gets more attention than the emotional consequences. Old had a great idea that could have made for an impactful film in the vein of Signs or The Sixth Sense , but it keeps finding ways to complicate the story without even making the twists all that interesting .

When you watch Don't Worry Darling , you easily understand the kind of criticism the movie is going for with its mix of sci-fi and psychological thriller elements . But while it's still an entertaining watch, the film gets a little lost in its own ideas. Here we follow Alice (Florence Pugh), a woman living with her husband, Jack (Harry Styles), in Victory, a perfect community inspired by '50s American suburbs. But while the men go to work for a mysterious company and the women spend their days taking care of their homes, Alice starts noticing that something isn't quite right. And what she eventually finds out is actually a great (but obvious) twist , touching on important issues such as abusive relationships and technology being used for manipulation. The problem is that it takes far too long to get there.

There's nothing wrong with taking your time to build a mystery, but there's a limit. By the time the big reveal finally happens, the film is already close to ending , leaving very little room to explore its consequences. So, some important questions get pushed aside: how exactly does this system work? And why doesn't the film do more with the situation between Alice and the people responsible for keeping her trapped in that place? Pugh's performance definitely helps, but even she can't make Don't Worry Darling a phenomenal feature on her own. It didn't need to explain every single detail, but it did need to do more with the ideas it had introduced.

The Circle is the kind of film you might watch once and never think about again. And that's a shame, since its premise has aged well. We meet Mae Holland (Emma Watson) , a young woman who lands a job at The Circle, one of the biggest tech companies in the world. Led by Eamon Bailey (Tom Hanks), this company develops a platform designed to bring together all of its users' information and activities, arguing that getting rid of privacy can make the world safer and more connected. Excited about the opportunity, Mae gets more involved in the company's projects and eventually decides to broadcast her whole life online, only to realize that this idea of total transparency can also be used to control and monitor people.

The concept has plenty of potential, as it talks about how much of our privacy we are willing to give up in exchange for convenience and security. You also can't help thinking how interesting it would be to see the story explore the ways a powerful company could influence people's behavior—but The Circle barely scratches the surface of any of these ideas. The protagonist's development isn't convincing, the company is more like a generic evil corporation, and the central conflict loses momentum right when it should be getting more complicated. The cast is solid, but the narrative never really pulls you in , which makes the whole thing disappointing. By the end, you feel like you've watched an incomplete movie.

The concept behind In Time is so good that, honestly, it could have worked better as a TV show or a full movie franchise—one film just wasn't enough to explore everything this world had to offer, which is why it's on this list. This dystopia imagines a future where people stop aging at 25 but are given just one more year to live, which they have to manage like money. In this world, time is literally currency: people work to earn more hours, pay for food and bills with minutes of their lives, while the wealthy can afford to accumulate decades or even centuries. It's a direct way of exploring social inequality . And the main character is Will Salas (Justin Timberlake), a man from a poor neighborhood who suddenly comes into a large amount of time and becomes a target for the authorities. His journey then turns into a fight against the system.

The problem with In Time is that it starts with an idea that makes economic inequality feel immediate: while the rich keep accumulating time, the poor are literally running out of life. But after setting this up, the script loses sight of what makes it compelling and turns into a fairly standard action movie, with car chases, shootouts, and a romance that gets more attention than the social issues that should be at the heart of it all. We get why those things were included, but maybe they would have worked better in a sequel. Ultimately, this is a production that never quite understood the size of what it had on its hands—one of the most creative concepts in sci-fi.

Anyone who remembers Passengers probably remembers that, much like In Time , it strays far from its original premise. However, in this case, it's an even bigger missed opportunity. The story takes place aboard the Avalon, a spaceship carrying 5,000 passengers on a 120-year journey to a distant planet. Everyone is supposed to remain in hibernation until they reach their destination, but a malfunction causes Jim Preston (Chris Pratt) to wake up 90 years too early. Unable to go back to sleep and realizing he'll spend the rest of his life alone, he loses hope and decides to wake up Aurora Lane (Jennifer Lawrence), another passenger, without telling her that he did it on purpose. So the two begin building a relationship while trying to figure out what went wrong with the ship.

Jim's decision should have been at the center of a debate about loneliness, selfishness, consent, and responsibility, right? But Passengers treats it more like an obstacle the couple needs to overcome before they can be together. Sure, the film is marketed as a sci-fi romance, but the idea had the potential to become the kind of story people would still be talking about and recommending today. Aurora has every reason to feel betrayed, since Jim didn't just take away her chance to reach the planet and start a new life; he made that decision for her without giving her a choice. This could have been a gripping psychological thriller because of that, and the ship could have played an important role as well, but the focus is on both characters trying to become a couple you're supposed to root for.

articles.title: Indian Auteur Girish Kasaravalli Looks Back on 50 Years of Cinema at IFFI Masterclass: 'All My Films Talk About Othering'
articles.summary: Indian auteur Girish Kasaravalli looked back on his career in Kannada-language cinema at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, in a masterclass titled "The Moral Universe of Parallel Cinema: 50 Years of Girish Kasaravalli." The 75-year-old spoke about the moral contradictions of society and the relationship between cinematic form and social […]
articles.content:
Indian auteur Girish Kasaravalli looked back on his career in Kannada-language cinema at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, in a masterclass titled "The Moral Universe of Parallel Cinema: 50 Years of Girish Kasaravalli."

The 75-year-old spoke about the moral contradictions of society and the relationship between cinematic form and social content. He also argued that even entertainment is a political act. The session was moderated by Variety 's Asia editor Naman Ramachandran. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Margot Robbie to Star in A24's 'The Week of Pain' From 'The Drama' Director Kristoffer Borgli Jo Koy on ‘Blue in the Face,’ Steven Spielberg, Biggie’s Mom and Learning What His Name Really Means at Long John Silver’s

Across films such as " Ghatashraddha " (1977), "Tabarana Kathe" (1986), "Thaayi Saheba" (1997), "Dweepa" (2002) and "Gulabi Talkies" (2008), Kasaravalli has kept returning to one question: how societies exclude individuals and communities, and how people who are themselves victims of oppressive structures can also become complicit in perpetuating them.

Asked whether the 1977 Kannada classic "Ghatashraddha," which examines religious orthodoxy and social exclusion, still spoke to contemporary India, Kasaravalli said: "All my films talk about othering. I always talk about how society looks at some people from a different lens, and in that process they make them 'other.'" He described this as "the biggest cruelty an individual or a group of people can impart on another person."

Asked whether he considered himself a political filmmaker, Kasaravalli said: "Whoever makes something, whether he makes mainstream cinema or art cinema, he is making a political statement, either in support of the dominant ideology or opposing the dominant ideology. He cannot avoid it." There is nothing called only entertainment, he added, and even entertainment is a political form. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

On his characters, he said: "I don't want any of my characters to become a kind of a mouthpiece to a certain ideology." Drawing on Jean-Luc Godard, he compared understanding a character to buying a house: one must examine it from the outside and then from within before making a judgment. Similarly, a filmmaker must inhabit a character and then step back to assess it. For Kasaravalli, characters are too complex for a filmmaker to easily take sides.

On the evolution of his cinematic language, Kasaravalli described the visual construction of "Ghatashraddha," as "ritualistic cinema." "The style is not imposed on it; it comes from within the content itself," he said. Since "Ghatashraddha" was about a ritual, he felt its cinematic form should reflect that structure.

Kasaravalli said he could not write a script until he had clarity about its images. "For me, the film is not merely making statements; it's an attempt by the filmmaker to impart an experience." He described writing detailed instructions for his crew, down to which hand a character uses to lift a glass, because even that changes the composition of a shot.

This attention to the relationship between character and environment shaped "Gulabi Talkies." Kasaravalli told cinematographer S. Ramachandra that the coastal community had to be as important as the protagonist. He wanted the images to feel like "actuality coverage," not a predetermined visual construction. Rejecting conventional scenic shots of the sea and rocks, he told his cinematographer: "Film should not have any pretty image." They chose 16mm, allowing the grain to contribute to the film's sense of actuality.

The discussion of visual aesthetics brought him to Cuban filmmaker Julio García Espinosa's idea of "imperfect cinema," which, for Kasaravalli, challenged the assumption that Western aesthetics should define cinematic perfection. "I don't want to take your aesthetic sensibility as my sensibility," he said, quoting Espinosa. Kasaravalli said each country and each region has its own aesthetic concerns. "We should make films according to that condition; we should never imitate the West. Why should I be perfect? I should be loyal to my own milieu."

Asked whether parallel cinema belonged to a particular period, Kasaravalli disagreed, pointing to notable films being made across the country today. The larger problem, he said, was reaching audiences. Of streaming platforms, he said: "We all thought it is going to be a solution for all of us. But OTT [streaming] is exactly doing what the mainstream distribution network was doing earlier." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In the audience Q&A, he addressed open endings and whether a filmmaker should provide answers. "A filmmaker who says that he knows answers for all the questions in life is telling a lie," he said. "He is also as confused as you are. He only throws up options so that you can start thinking. There is nothing called closure… life is always open."

As the session concluded, IFFI festival director Ashutosh Gowariker described Kasaravalli's work as "textbooks," saying he had returned to "Ghatashraddha" while developing a new film. He also singled out the filmmaker's close-ups. "You let your actors simply be. You make the audience think and anticipate what the character is going through," Gowariker said.

"I don’t know anything about the movies we're gonna see, I haven’t seen a single image," the Oscar-winning actor said at the fest's jury press conference on Saturday morning. "That’s how I love to see movies, I don’t want to have any information." articles.title: What Is the Most Misunderstood '80s Sci-Fi Movie? There's a Clear Answer
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Orion Pictures I love a good science-fiction movie that gives you something to think about after the explosions stop. The 1980s had plenty of them, from Blade Runner to The Terminator. But there's one movie that seems to get remembered for all the wrong reasons. It's violent, occasionally ridiculous, and has a giant metal man who shoots […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google I love a good science-fiction movie that gives you something to think about after the explosions stop. The 1980s had plenty of them, from Blade Runner to The Terminator . But there's one movie that seems to get remembered for all the wrong reasons. It's violent, occasionally ridiculous, and has a giant metal man who shoots criminals in the face. What's not to love? Yet there's considerably more going on beneath all that mayhem. In fact, I think one of the decade's most entertaining sci-fi movies also happens to be one of its sharpest social satires.

Paul Verhoeven wasn't exactly interested in making another straightforward action movie. He had something much nastier in mind. His vision of the future was full of corporate greed, television sensationalism, and people who had apparently decided that everything was better when somebody could make money from it. There's also a surprisingly heartbreaking story hiding underneath the mechanical armor. And that's why I think RoboCop deserves another look.

Released in 1987, RoboCop introduced audiences to Alex Murphy, a Detroit police officer who gets brutally murdered by a gang led by Clarence Boddicker. His remains become the foundation for a new crime-fighting machine developed by Omni Consumer Products. The company wants to take over Detroit's police force and sees Murphy's transformation as a wonderful business opportunity. There's just one little problem. Murphy hasn't entirely disappeared. Memories of his former life begin returning, and the supposedly obedient machine starts looking rather inconvenient for the people who built him. Peter Weller does some terrific work here. He manages to make a character covered in metal feel like a real person struggling to understand what happened to him. That's not exactly easy when most of your face is hidden behind a futuristic helmet of a RoboCop . Check out this trailer and see for yourself.

Of course, Verhoeven also makes sure there's plenty of outrageous fun along the way. The commercials for bizarre products and the news reports about increasingly ridiculous disasters give the movie a wonderfully nasty sense of humor. Then there's the infamous demonstration of ED-209, which goes spectacularly wrong during a corporate presentation. It's one of the funniest scenes in the entire movie. But there's a reason these moments work so well. Verhoeven isn't just throwing random jokes into an action film. He's showing us a society where corporate executives treat human lives like another line on a balance sheet. The violence is deliberately excessive, and the humor makes the whole thing even more uncomfortable. RoboCop wants you to laugh.

The thing I find most interesting about RoboCop isn't actually the political satire. It's Murphy himself. Before the company turned him into a walking weapons platform, he was a husband, a father, and a police officer who thought he was doing something worthwhile. Now he's expected to follow instructions and protect a corporation's interests. His memories don't fit neatly into that arrangement. Watching Murphy slowly recover pieces of his identity gives the movie an emotional center that plenty of action films would have ignored. There's a particularly effective sadness to his attempts to remember his family. He can still recognize fragments of his old life, but he can't simply return to it. That's a pretty bleak idea for a movie that also features a giant robot shooting people during a boardroom presentation. Weller deserves a lot of credit for making both sides of the character work.

It's also worth remembering that RoboCop wasn't universally dismissed when it arrived. Roger Ebert gave it a positive review in 1987 and recognized the unusual combination of comedy, philosophy, and social commentary. Other critics struggled more with its mixture of genres and graphic violence. That confusion has largely disappeared as the movie's reputation has grown. Yet I still think people sometimes focus on the wrong things when discussing it. The film's corporate satire feels remarkably relevant, but its story about a man fighting to reclaim his humanity is what gives it staying power. Verhoeven would explore similar ideas in Total Recall and Starship Troopers , but there's something especially effective about the way he brings them together here. RoboCop may have been built like a big, noisy action movie. Underneath all that steel was a much sadder story. And that's the part I think deserves more attention.

And what do you guys think? Is this series really misunderstood? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title: Marvel Delivered Its Most Terrifying MCU Villain 11 Years Ago, And He Broke the TV Series That Created Him
articles.summary: The Marvel Cinematic Universe has had its fair share of impressive and imposing villains throughout its 18 years of existence. Killmonger had an understandable motivation and was so tough that he actually took over as Black Panther for a time. The High Evolutionary didn't care who or what he harmed to get what he wanted. […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The Marvel Cinematic Universe has had its fair share of impressive and imposing villains throughout its 18 years of existence. Killmonger had an understandable motivation and was so tough that he actually took over as Black Panther for a time. The High Evolutionary didn't care who or what he harmed to get what he wanted. Even the often heroic Wanda Maximoff proved to be a terrifying antagonist in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness . Of course, Thanos literally snapped away half of all life and defeated the Avengers. Despite all those villains, the scariest one in the history of the franchise debuted in 2015.

That antagonist is sometimes known as the Purple Man and he's the main villain for Jessica Jones to combat. The character was the focal point of the inaugural season of Jessica Jones on Netflix, which is often forgotten about by many people because it hasn't played a major part in the greater MCU. Outside of the titular character returning in Daredevil: Born Again , it hasn't mattered all that much. The Purple Man is also known as Kilgrave and he was so frightening that once he was gone, the show couldn't find that same level of success or quality.

If you looked at Kilgrave and knew nothing else about him, you wouldn't think he could be considered the MCU's scariest bad guy . Played by the incredibly talented David Tennant, Kilgrave looks like an everyday dude. He wears a suit, is relatively thin, and couldn't beat up most people. He's certainly no match for the powerful Jessica Jones from a physicality standpoint. What makes him so scary is his ability to control minds and make people do whatever he wants by simply telling them what to do. Taking away someone's agency is one of the most evil and scary things you could do.

Before we even see Kilgrave, we see the effects of his powers. He held Hope Shlottman captive, sexually abused her, and told her to kill her parents. When we actually see him (though not his face at this point), he takes over a family's house and forces them to do whatever he says. We also learn that he enslaved Jessica for a time in the past, using her for sex and whatever else he wanted. Kilgrave did this all without any remorse and didn't even see anything wrong with it. He believed that Jessica wanted to be with him, while she had suffered from PTSD after breaking away from him.

Every scene with Kilgrave was rife with tension. You always watched nervously, knowing that he could destroy lives in an instant. When he escapes Jessica's capture midway through Season 1, he tells Jessica's best friend Trish to shoot herself in the head. It's a terrifying scene that only has a somewhat happy ending because the gun was empty. Seeing Jessica, one of the strongest MCU heroes physically and mentally, showcase such a sense of fear around Kilgrave sold his villain status even more. Their dynamic helped make Jessica Jones Season 1 one of the best seasons of Marvel television ever produced.

Almost everyone who reads Jessica Jones comic books tends to agree that Kilgrave is her greatest enemy. The stories surrounding him and Jessica are so captivating that the comics ran into a problem where they couldn't quite deliver tales nearly as good without him. The Netflix series had the same trouble. While Season 1 of Jessica Jones was brilliant, the show couldn't find a villain anywhere near as compelling in the two following seasons. Season 2 was praised for the performances and the focus on female characters, but Jessica's mom returning never grabbed audiences the way Kilgrave did.

Jessica Jones Season 3 expanded on Trish's story and saw her utilize her enhanced abilities to become a vigilante. It also gave us an intense and highly intelligent psychopath as the villain, but as dangerous as he was, nothing really came close to how Kilgrave's scenes felt. In a lot of ways, Jessica Jones may have benefitted from starting with other villains before moving on to Kilgrave, as he's a nearly impossible act to follow, which the comics have proven. The fact that Kilgrave could be as scary as he was on a streaming service that saw Kingpin dominating screens at the same time is a testament to how chilling the character is.

As a whole, Jessica Jones is a very strong show. Krysten Ritter gave great performances over each episode, and while it was never bad, it certainly peaked during that first season. Kilgrave was a big part of that because the best thing you can do for a great superhero story is to give them someone absolutely terrifying to face off against. Kilgrave's ability to scare us without being physically imposing is something you felt in your bones and is something no other MCU villain can match.

Do you think there's a scarier MCU antagonist than Kilgrave? Let us know your picks in the comments.

articles.title: 3 Unadaptable Sci-Fi Books That Actually Became Great Movies (But One Took Multiple Attempts)
articles.summary: The label “unadaptable” has been slapped onto many works of literature over the years, especially in science fiction. Since the birth of the film industry in 1895, studios, producers, and filmmakers have been trying to film the unfilmable, finding creative ways to capture complex worlds and internal struggles with cinematic visuals. Historically, when someone attempts […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The label “unadaptable” has been slapped onto many works of literature over the years, especially in science fiction . Since the birth of the film industry in 1895, studios, producers, and filmmakers have been trying to film the unfilmable, finding creative ways to capture complex worlds and internal struggles with cinematic visuals. Historically, when someone attempts to adapt an “unadaptable” story, detractors, fans, and sometimes even the authors of the original works come out against the project, claiming it can’t be done.

But as the following films prove, telling Hollywood it can’t do something only adds fuel to the fire. Regardless of previous stalled projects or failed attempts, a visionary filmmaker eventually steps up to the plate, ready to take on the challenge. The result, at least in these cases, is a masterful mind-bending tale or sweeping science fiction odyssey that wows audiences in theaters and becomes a home-viewing classic that stands the test of time.

Watchmen began as a 12-issue comic series from DC, written by Alan Moore and illustrated by Dave Gibbons. But Moore himself argued that Watchmen wasn’t cinematic, noting that a comic reader can flip back and connect details, while film forces you to watch at 24 frames per second. Another problem was the scope. After Moore declined to write the screenplay, screenwriter Sam Hamm attempted to squeeze the 338-page comic into a 128-page script. When the project moved to Warner Bros., it attached sci-fi master Terry Gilliam, who was unhappy with Hamm’s script, bringing in Charles McKeown to rewrite it using Rorschach’s journal as voice-over. Although it seemed they’d gotten closer, Gilliam’s film also collapsed over budget, and later drafts by David Hayter replaced it.

Warner Bros. eventually hired director Zack Snyder in 2006, and the rest is history. Snyder pulled it off by using the comic itself as his storyboard. He added a title montage to explain the alternate history, and used a simplified ending taken from Hayter. Moore himself ultimately took no credit for the film and gave his share of the income to Gibbons. Gibbons said that watching it on DVD would feel like flipping through the book, since viewers could pause and rewind, and he was right: DVD sales are where Watchmen made its money back. Today, Watchmen is considered a superhero sci-fi classic, and it even launched a Watchmen sequel series from Damon Lindelof .

Philip K. Dick’s A Scanner Darkly entranced readers with the story of an undercover cop in a near-future world who gets involved with a dangerous new drug and begins to lose his identity. However, Dick’s writing is known for being extremely internal, leading readers through the breakdown of the protagonist’s perception from the inside; something nearly impossible to show visually on screen. Director Richard Linklater, who had experimented with rotoscoping on Waking Life , was interested in adapting one of Dick’s novels. He first played around with Ubik , but eventually turned to A Scanner Darkly , deciding to direct it as an intimate animated sci-fi thriller, made for only $8.7 million. His script followed the novel closely, and when he pitched it to Dick’s estate, it was approved.

It was ultimately Linklater’s rotoscoped animation that was key to the film’s success. The technique involved filming live actors (including Keanu Reeves, Robert Downey Jr., Woody Harrelson, and Winona Ryder), then having animators paint over the footage frame by frame. The result is a shifting, dreamlike animation that conveys the character’s fragmented, drug-induced perception while still allowing the actors to give live performances. Instead of turning it into a big-budget action thriller, Linklater leaned into the story's internal nature, helming what is now considered not only a cult classic, but one of the more successful Dick adaptations and one of Linklater’s most unique films.

Frank Herbert’s space opera opus Dune built out an entire galaxy’s politics, theology, ecology, and characters. The first notable adaptation attempt came when director Alejandro Jodorowsky began plotting his film, which included music by Pink Floyd and a dream cast of Orson Welles, Salvador Dalí, and Mick Jagger. Trouble was, Jodorowsky’s script would have made a 14-hour movie, and he’d already spent $2 million of the $9 million budget on pre-production. Thus, the project stalled. Next, Ridley Scott was hired to direct and was the first to consider splitting the book into two films. However, Scott’s version focused on an incestuous relationship, which outraged Herbert, and Scott ultimately dropped the project to make Blade Runner . David Lynch then became the first to put the book on screen, though he famously didn’t get final cut, and the result was so disastrous that Lynch disowned the film.

Enter modern-day sci-fi master Denis Villeneuve. Following the idea Scott first floated, he split the story into two films. Using minimal dialogue, he relied on largely practical visual world-building and took a restrained approach to adapting the story and characters, leaving the audience to build out much of the world for themselves without over-explaining the complicated lore and terminology. His adaptations have finally proven a success, making the unfilmable filmable, with Dune: Part Two making over $714 million worldwide. His upcoming Dune: Part Three , based on the next novel, Dune Messiah , is set to open in December as the final film in the trilogy.

Are there any sci-fi novels you think are truly unfilmable? Let us know in the comments below.
